children.text: The Policy Origin: CMS-9115-F and the Interoperability Mandate

On May 1, 2020, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services published the landmark Interoperability and Patient Access final rule, formally known as CMS-9115-F. The rule arrived amid a pandemic, yet it represented years of policymaking work aimed at dismantling one of the most persistent barriers in American healthcare: the inability of patients to easily obtain and move their own health data. For decades, insurance claims, encounter records, and clinical results sat locked inside payer systems, accessible only through cumbersome request processes. CMS-9115-F changed the legal landscape fundamentally by requiring regulated payers to open standardized, secure digital doors directly to patients and the applications patients choose.

The rule applies to a broad set of federally regulated payers: Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations, Medicaid Fee-for-Service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Fee-for-Service programs, CHIP managed care entities, and issuers of Qualified Health Plans (QHPs) on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges. This scope is intentional — together these programs cover hundreds of millions of Americans, and establishing a uniform standard across them creates the critical mass needed to make patient-facing data exchange a market reality rather than a pilot curiosity. Notably, large commercial plans sold outside the exchanges were not directly captured, a gap that some states have moved to close through their own legislation.

The technical standard chosen by CMS was HL7 FHIR Release 4.0.1, the then-current version of the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources specification. FHIR R4 provides a REST-based API architecture with well-defined resource types, enabling developers to build consumer applications without requiring bespoke integrations for each payer. CMS recognized implementation complexity created by the COVID-19 pandemic and exercised enforcement discretion through July 1, 2021, at which point active enforcement of the Patient Access API and Provider Directory API requirements began in earnest. Missing either deadline was not a technicality — CMS signaled it would use existing program oversight authorities, including corrective action plans and, for Medicare Advantage, contract termination.

children.text: What the Patient Access API Must Expose

The Patient Access API is not a single data dump — it is a structured set of FHIR resource endpoints that collectively give a member a longitudinal view of what their insurance plan knows about them. CMS-9115-F identified three primary categories of data that must be available: claims and encounter information (including cost data such as provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing), clinical data including laboratory results when maintained by the payer, and formulary and coverage data. The CARIN Alliance for Blue Button Implementation Guide (CARIN IG) was explicitly endorsed by CMS as the recommended specification for the claims and encounter data layer, defining profiles for the Patient, Coverage, and ExplanationOfBenefit FHIR resources that form the foundation of every compliant implementation.

The clinical data requirement is where many payer implementations have stumbled. CMS requires that payers expose data classes and elements aligned with the U.S. Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) standard, as reflected in the US Core FHIR Implementation Guide. This means exposing resources such as MedicationRequest, Condition, Procedure, and CareTeam — data elements that can logically be derived from claims even when payers do not hold provider-sourced clinical records. CMS-0057-F (the 2024 successor rule) escalated the bar by requiring conformance with USCDI v3, a step up from the USCDI v1 that most CMS-9115-F implementations targeted. In practice, fewer than 30 percent of evaluated payer APIs made clinical resources fully available, illustrating how the clinical data tier remains the most challenging compliance frontier.

Access to this data is member-authorized and flows through the OAuth 2.0 SMART App Launch protocol, which allows a member to grant a third-party application permission to retrieve their records directly from the payer's FHIR server. The application receives a token scoped to that member's data, and the payer must return the applicable FHIR resources without filtering or degrading the data. CMS explicitly prohibits payers from using the app registration process as a competitive gatekeeping mechanism — registration must be open to any legitimate developer, and delays or denials without documented security justification constitute compliance violations.

children.text: Payer-to-Payer Data Exchange: From CMS-9115-F to CMS-0057-F

One of the most ambitious provisions of the original CMS-9115-F was the requirement that payers exchange data with each other when a member transitions between plans. The vision: when you switch from one insurance plan to another, your new insurer automatically receives up to five years of your claims, encounter, and clinical history from your prior insurer — reducing redundant testing, filling dangerous care gaps, and enabling your new care team to understand your complete medical story from day one. However, implementation challenges proved severe. On December 8, 2021, CMS announced enforcement discretion on the payer-to-payer provisions of CMS-9115-F, acknowledging that the member-mediated authentication model outlined in the original rule was not well-suited for business-to-business data transfers.

The 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F), published January 17, 2024, resolved these tensions with a redesigned Payer-to-Payer API framework. Under CMS-0057-F, payers are no longer required to use patient-mediated SMART App Launch authentication for payer-to-payer exchanges — CMS recognized that "protocols requiring user level credentials managed by the payer are generally not appropriate for business-to-business data exchanges." Instead, the new model requires that when a member enrolls in a new plan, the receiving payer must collect the member's opt-in consent and information about former or concurrent plans, then — within one week of receiving both — request the required data from identified prior payers. The full Payer-to-Payer API compliance deadline under CMS-0057-F is January 1, 2027.

The technical vehicle for payer-to-payer exchange is the Da Vinci Payer Data Exchange (PDex) Implementation Guide, which CMS recommends as the specification for this API. PDex defines how payers package FHIR resources — including claims, USCDI clinical data, and prior authorization history — into standardized bundles that receiving payers can ingest. A critical feature of PDex is its provenance framework, which preserves the chain of custody for clinical information as it moves across payer boundaries. The data scope is substantial: up to five years of adjudicated claims and encounters (excluding provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing), data classes aligned with USCDI, and prior authorization information excluding drug authorizations. Plain-language educational resources explaining the Payer-to-Payer API to members must also be provided, underscoring that member trust and informed consent are foundational to the design.

body.analogy: Imagine every time you moved to a new city, your entire medical file automatically transferred to your new doctor's office before your first appointment — without you having to carry a folder of records or repeat your history from scratch.
body.concept: The Payer-to-Payer API aims to create the same seamless longitudinal data continuity when members change insurance plans, ensuring new payers and providers start with a complete picture instead of a blank slate.

children.text: The Provider Directory API: Making Network Data Trustworthy

Alongside the Patient Access API, CMS-9115-F required covered payers to implement a publicly accessible, FHIR R4-based Provider Directory API. The purpose is straightforward but long-elusive: give consumers, providers, and app developers reliable, machine-readable information about which clinicians and facilities participate in a given insurance network. The implementation guide endorsed by CMS for this purpose is the Da Vinci PDEX Plan-Net IG, currently at version 1.2.0 (published February 25, 2025). Plan-Net defines FHIR profiles for the key entities in a provider network: Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Organization, OrganizationAffiliation, HealthcareService, InsurancePlan, Endpoint, and Location. Together these resources allow a third-party application to answer questions like "Which cardiologists in Burlington, Vermont accept my Blue Cross plan?"

Provider directory accuracy has been a chronic industry problem, and the No Surprises Act — which took effect January 1, 2022 — added regulatory teeth by creating a 90-day attestation cycle. Health plans must verify all provider details at least once every 90 days, including physician name, specialty, address, phone number, and network participation status. Inaccurate directories create concrete patient harm: a member who selects an in-network provider based on a stale directory and then receives an unexpected out-of-network bill has experienced both a financial injury and a failure of the information infrastructure that was supposed to protect them. CMS reinforced this with Medicare Advantage-specific requirements for annual attestation of directory accuracy through the HPMS MPF Provider Directory module, adding a formal accountability mechanism to what had previously been an honor-system process.

Despite mandatory requirements, the state of provider directory FHIR APIs as of 2024 remains uneven. Many payers have struggled to maintain accurate Practitioner-to-Plan relationships — one of the most frequently cited deficiencies in API audits. The core challenge is organizational: provider directory data is collected through credentialing, contracting, and roster processes that often exist in siloed systems. Surfacing this data through a coherent FHIR API requires not only technical integration work but also operational governance to ensure that roster updates flow promptly into the API. CMS-0057-F introduced a Provider Access API — distinct from the public-facing Provider Directory API — that allows providers to query payer data about their own patients, with a separate compliance deadline of January 1, 2027.

body.message: A "ghost network" occurs when a provider appears in an insurance directory but is no longer accepting new patients, has left the network, or has moved locations. Studies have found error rates exceeding 40 percent in some commercial plan directories. The Provider Directory API requirement creates a machine-readable surface for auditing — but the data quality it reflects is only as good as the operational processes feeding it.
body.title: Ghost Networks: A Persistent Patient Safety Problem

body.content: A developer querying a compliant Plan-Net endpoint can retrieve a PractitionerRole resource that bundles the practitioner's NPI, specialty taxonomy code, the specific InsurancePlan network they participate in, their office address as a Location resource, accepted patient telephones, and the network's HealthcareService offerings — all in a single structured FHIR response. This is the machine-readable equivalent of the printed directory booklet, updated continuously rather than annually.

children.text: Adoption, Enforcement, and the Gaps That Remain

More than four years after the July 2021 enforcement date, the Patient Access API landscape reflects the messy reality of federal mandates meeting real-world implementation complexity. Industry analysis published in November 2024 by Flexpa found that nearly half of targeted payer endpoints still lacked a live, conformant Patient Access API, and that actual member usage — the number of API calls being made by consumers through third-party apps — numbered in the hundreds per plan rather than the thousands that would indicate mainstream adoption. The contrast with established health information networks is stark: Carequality moves approximately 940 million clinical documents per month through provider-initiated queries, while patient-mediated FHIR pulls via the Patient Access API are orders of magnitude smaller.

CMS enforcement has been measured rather than aggressive. The agency uses existing program oversight mechanisms — annual survey instruments for Medicare Advantage, the QHP certification process for Marketplace plans, and state-level oversight for Medicaid and CHIP — rather than a centralized enforcement unit issuing fines. Enforcement actions can escalate from corrective action plans to public reporting of violations and ultimately to contract termination for Medicare Advantage organizations, but documented cases of termination specifically for Patient Access API non-compliance remain rare. CMS did, however, signal a new accountability lever: starting January 1, 2026, impacted payers must annually report Patient Access API usage metrics to CMS (first report due March 31, 2026), creating a transparency mechanism that will enable comparative assessment of engagement across plans.

Perhaps the most consequential unresolved gap is the privacy protection asymmetry for data that leaves the payer system. When a member authorizes a third-party app to receive their health data through the Patient Access API, that data exits the HIPAA regulatory perimeter. Most third-party health apps are not covered entities and are not bound by HIPAA — they are instead subject to the Federal Trade Commission Act, which prohibits deceptive practices but does not constrain how a company may use or monetize health data as long as its privacy policy discloses those practices. This creates a scenario where a member's complete insurance claims history — a detailed proxy for their medical conditions, prescriptions, and provider relationships — could lawfully be sold to data brokers or used for targeted advertising, with the only safeguard being whatever terms the app's privacy policy contains. The ONC and FTC have flagged this gap repeatedly, but as of mid-2025 no federal legislation has closed it comprehensively.

The state-level response has begun to fill some voids. California's SB 1419, effective January 1, 2025, and Tennessee's SB 2012, effective May 2024, extended Patient Access API-style requirements to commercial plans sold outside the federally facilitated exchanges — populations not covered by CMS-9115-F. These state actions are early indicators that interoperability mandates may eventually reach all lines of business, not just government-program-adjacent markets. Meanwhile, the January 2027 deadline under CMS-0057-F for the full suite of new APIs — Payer-to-Payer, Provider Access, and Prior Authorization — represents the next major wave of compliance pressure that will test whether payers can scale from partial Patient Access API conformance to a comprehensive interoperability architecture.

children.text: What This Means for Vermont's Health Ecosystem

Vermont's health system occupies a distinctive position in the national interoperability landscape. The state operates a unified Health Information Exchange (Vermont HIE/VHIE) and has long pursued All-Payer Model ambitions that require rich data flows between payers, providers, and the state itself. For Green Mountain Care Board-regulated payers and the Vermont Health Connect marketplace, the CMS-9115-F and CMS-0057-F requirements overlay on top of existing state data-sharing expectations. Vermont Blue Cross Blue Shield, MVP Health Care, and Medicaid managed care organizations operating in the state are all subject to the federal Patient Access API mandates and must maintain conformant FHIR endpoints serving members.

The practical implication for Vermont consumers is significant but still largely unrealized. A Vermont resident enrolled in Medicaid or a Marketplace plan today has the legal right to connect any SMART-on-FHIR application to their payer's Patient Access API and retrieve their complete claims history, formulary information, and available clinical data. Yet awareness of this right is minimal, and the ecosystem of trustworthy, Vermont-specific health management apps built on these APIs is nascent. Closing the gap between legal entitlement and consumer benefit requires not just API compliance but also member education, app vetting frameworks, and policy clarity on downstream data use protections that Vermont could model through state-level privacy legislation.

For healthcare organizations and technologists building on Vermont's health platform, the Patient Access API represents an underutilized data source. Aggregating member-authorized payer data alongside provider-sourced clinical data from the VHIE creates the longitudinal health record that care coordination programs need but have historically lacked. Population health analytics, care gap identification, and medication reconciliation all improve meaningfully when claims data — the most complete record of what services a member actually received — is available alongside clinical documentation. The CMS-0057-F Payer-to-Payer API will further amplify this by ensuring that members who transition between Vermont plans or arrive in Vermont from out of state bring their prior history with them automatically.

The Patient Access API is not an IT project. It is a patient rights framework built on top of an IT standard. The goal is not API uptime — it is a Vermont where every resident can walk into any healthcare encounter with their complete insurance and clinical history in hand.

points: CMS-9115-F (published May 1, 2020) required Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and QHP payers to implement FHIR R4-based Patient Access APIs; enforcement began July 1, 2021.

The Patient Access API must expose claims and encounter data via CARIN Blue Button-profiled FHIR resources (ExplanationOfBenefit, Coverage, Patient), plus USCDI-aligned clinical data and formulary information.
CMS-0057-F (January 2024) replaced the original payer-to-payer provisions, establishing a business-to-business API model with opt-in consent and a January 1, 2027 compliance deadline.
The Payer-to-Payer API carries up to five years of claims, encounters, USCDI clinical data, and prior authorization history, using the DaVinci PDex IG for packaging and provenance.

The Da Vinci PDEX Plan-Net IG (current version 1.2.0, February 2025) defines the FHIR-based Provider Directory API, which the No Surprises Act reinforced with mandatory 90-day data attestation cycles.
Actual member adoption of third-party apps connecting to Patient Access APIs remains low — hundreds of pulls per plan versus hundreds of millions of provider-initiated transactions monthly.

Health data shared through the Patient Access API exits HIPAA protections once received by a non-covered third-party app; FTC oversight covers only deceptive practices, leaving a significant privacy gap.
Starting March 31, 2026, payers must report annual Patient Access API usage metrics to CMS — creating the first systematic transparency tool for measuring real-world engagement.

body.explanation: CMS endorsed the CARIN Alliance for Blue Button Implementation Guide as the recommended specification for surfacing claims and encounter data through the Patient Access API. This IG defines profiles for the Patient, Coverage, and ExplanationOfBenefit FHIR resources that form the backbone of every compliant payer implementation. The PDex IG serves a different but related role — it is recommended for the Payer-to-Payer API context, particularly for provenance tracking when data moves between plans.
